that the second report of the standing committee on privileges and elections presented on June 15, 1964 be now concurred in.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, parliamentary
fortune of the second report of the standing committee on privileges and elections has long been delayed. It is my earnest hope that the healing power of time has composed whatever differences there may have been over its acceptance. This inquest into the past has deeply exercised the minds of many members, and its evolution from its origin has been in a sea of controversy.
If it is not inconvenient or disagreeable to the house, may I be allowed to offer a few observations. It is scarcely necessary for me to make plain that I speak only for myself. It would be convenient, I think, if I began by reintroducing the history of the matter for the house in a very summary fashion, and by this means we may retrace our steps.
It will be remembered that on April 27 last the hon. member for Labelle rose on a point of privilege and made a statement to the house which included the gist of an alleged conversation between the national organizer of the Liberal party and himself in the presence of four other hon. members. Perhaps due to provocation, the statement was couched in language that readily lent itself to misconstruction.

In any event, Mr. Speaker, I shall not trust to my memory. I would like to refer textually to Hansard at page 2645, where the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is reported as saying:
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the member for Labelle has alleged in this house that he was offered a bribe...It is a breach of the privileges of this House of Commons...

Privileges and Elections Committee
That constituted the first allegation that accompanied the motion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. If I may, I should like to go on now to page 2646 of Hansard where the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre continued as follows:
The hon. member for Labelle has been insulted by the alleged offer of a bribe. The Prime Minister has been insulted by what the hon. member for Labelle said about him...But my concern is that an insult to any member of the House of Commons is an insult to the house as a whole.
Once these allegations were turned loose, Mr. Speaker, a burden of suspicion fell upon all parties concerned, and it is a melancholy thing to see good names and honourable reputations trampled into the ground. It would be appropriate, I suggest, that the house remind itself of what is contained within the report. I do not propose to read all the report but only two material sentences:
Your committee reports that it found no evidence of bribery or attempted bribery. There was no question of privilege involved in the present reference.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we ought to do everything within our power to undo the injustice that has been done, and in the course of my submission I shall respectfully invite the house to accept the report of one of its own committees as the considered judgment of the entire house. Before I turn to deal very briefly with the evidence on which the report rests I desire to dispel the innuendoes arising from alleged reports of the happenings at the chance and casual meeting which took place at Hull on the evening of February 17.
I am pleased to emphasize that the conduct of every member present was not unworthy of the standard expected of members in this chamber. As I approach the evidence it will be my earnest endeavour as well as my earnest desire to approach it in a detached and impartial manner. In fairness to the hon. member for Labelle I must say he made it abundantly clear, at the earliest opportunity before the committee, that he did not rise with the intention of accusing anyone or anything. I would ask the house to turn to page 50 in the first volume of the proceedings before the committee where the hon. member is reported as follows:
-when I rose on a question of privilege I did not rise with the intention of accusing anyone or anything.

speechtext:
That is correct.
It is my respectful submission that no matter how you look at the evidence of the hon. member for Labelle you are driven back to the conclusion reached by the committee.
It is only fit and proper that I should make reference to the evidence of the hon. member for York-Scarborough and of the national organizer of the Liberal party. Both confirm the evidence of the hon. member for Labelle that there had been no attempt to bribe him. The force of the evidence when viewed dispassionately and with a single desire to see that justice is done dissipates and destroys every particle of the allegation of bribery.
I now pass to the second allegation, which might best be described as nothing more than the ghost of a rumour wrapped up in hearsay four times removed. It was a paradox, however, that the committee had to accept that, while they were called upon to investigate a question of privilege they found there was no question of privilege to investigate.
Let me go back to the report which I have already read to the house: "There is no question of bribery involved in the present

reference". The committee looked at all the circumstances and considered the evidence with care and precision, but came to the honest conclusion that the point involved was outside the definition of a question of privilege as we understand it in this house. May I say we were not unmindful of the attractive and persuasive argument put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but the committee also had the advice of the learned parliamentary counsel who was in attendance throughout.
I might reasonably anticipate that this part of the report may become a target for criticism because the committee did not return a formal verdict as to the truth or falsity of the allegation. The answer to such criticism is simplicity itself. Once the committee, after careful and conscientious consideration, had reached the conclusion that there was no question of privilege involved, then it would have been in violation of its principles to have taken the matter further. But I am bold enough to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is in this part of the report that may be found the real and lasting fruits of the committee's efforts. If out of the experience of the committee we serve to stiffen the resolution of this house not to spend its energies in pursuing synthetic points of privilege, then the committee will have been proved a useful instrument.
In the peculiar and special circumstances of this case I would be doing a great injustice to hon. members on both sides of the house if I were to let the matter rest there. It is within the knowledge of the house that on April 28 the right hon. Prime Minister rose in this house and categorically denied that there was any truth in this allegation. I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that all reasonable and fair minded members on both sides of the house will agree that the Prime Minister's denial was an unanswerable reply to a contrary suggestion. It would be contrary, however, to the canons of decency and fair play if I did not also bring to your attention the fact that the hon. member for Labelle, while he denied that he was the original author of the allegation, at least was frank enough to concede that he did not suggest there was any truth in the allegation. The hon. member for York-Scarborough, while he also entered a personal disclaimer as to the authorship of this allegation, also stated- and was joined by the national organizer of the Liberal party-that there was no truth in this suggestion.

Whatever may be the fate of this motion, Mr. Speaker, at least I am entitled to claim that before the committee not one word was subtracted from the statement the Prime Minister made in this house on April 28.
I come for a brief moment to another matter that excited some difference of opinion within the committee, when the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), as was his right, in a somewhat aggressive and hostile fashion took exception to the suggestion that the committee should terminate its hearings upon the evidence of only three witnesses. However, the contrary point of view put forth by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) carried conviction to the mind of the committee and eventually commanded its assent. I can do no better than to borrow his words, which may be found on page 278 of the fourth volume of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee:
It is now obvious that we are almost certain to have the word of five persons against the word of one which, to a general attitude towards fair play, looks unsatisfactory to everyone; that is, five to one in terms of this question of whether or not there were enticements.. .1 think we would be stupid to go much further in trying to nail this particular thing down. It seems to me that it is going to be a question of one man's word against five other men's word.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not dissociate myself from those remarks. On the contrary, I fully and wholeheartedly approve.
I come now to my final observation, and I move on to more debatable grounds. The house is acutely aware that there was a violent collision between the evidence given under oath by the hon. member for Labelle on the one hand and that given under oath by the hon. member for York-Scarborough and the national organizer of the Liberal party on the other. I would be failing in my duty, Mr. Speaker, if I attempted to pass over in silence this conflict in the evidence. I candidly confess that if you viewed this antagonism through the spectacles of suspicion, in a spirit of hostility and mistrust, then it is open to the harshest construction and must lead to the most prejudicial conclusion. But the first principle of justice demands that we view this matter in the most favourable light. It is my humble submission that if we approach this problem in a reasonable manner, making reasonable conclusions and reasonable assumptions, then the knot of entangled evidence may be untied with honour and with freedom of conscience.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to disfigure my few remarks with egotism, but perhaps the house will allow me to say that I have spent

Privileges and Elections Committee a large measure of my life within a courtroom, and I do not find the circumstances now engaging the attention of the house particularly unusual. More than 100 years ago a great judge of the common law dealt with this problem in this language:
It is a matter of frequent observation that persons dwelling for a long time on facts which they believe must have occurred come at last to persuade themselves that they do actually recollect the occurrences of circumstances which at first they only begin by believing must have happened. Without imputing anything like wilful and corrupt perjury to witnesses they often in truth bona fide believe that they have heard and remembered conversations which in truth never existed.
This was the language of Sir John Romilly, attorney general and solicitor general in Great Britain and a judge of the high court. It is no exaggeration to say that his judgment has been confirmed from that day until this moment. I am confident that the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) out of his own experiences will confirm the authority which I have just cited. If he will allow me, I would adopt his words which he used before the committee and which are to be found at page 279 of the fourth volume of the committee report. They are as follows:
Of course it Is not unusual in any tribunal, whether it is a committee such as this where you call a witness, or a board or even a court, to find that witnesses differ. For example, it happens often in a court of law that one witness in a vehicle accident says he was on the right side of the road going in the one direction and another witness says he was on the other side going in another direction and all this happened on a 66 foot highway, and both of them have a head on collision almost at a standstill.
It should be borne in mind, Mr. Speaker, that these witnesses were asked to cast their minds back over a period of some two and a half months to recapture and reconstruct conversations and events which occurred at a time when no one thought they would ever be called into dispute.
I may reasonably anticipate, Mr. Speaker, that it will be said: "Put the law into action", but I can only answer that I can find no law to put into action. I do not say this to escape an unpleasant situation or for purposes of expediency, for if I felt otherwise I would not falter for one moment to oppose this report. May I say to the house that if we continue to bandy this report about it will become the cemetery for the good names and honourable reputations of innocent people. In my respectful submission the house can accept this report without mortgaging its conscience.
Let me say this and only this. Less than two years ago I came into this chamber for

the first time believing it to be the highest court in the land. I came believing it was a court not only of legislation but a court of justice and of honour. It is in that firm belief that I now invite the house to accept the report in the spirit and the letter in which it was tabled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my delay in rising was that I had assumed that the hon. member for Bow River was getting to his feet to participate in this stage of the debate.
Before going into the main object of my remarks on this report I think as one who served on the committee I would first of all like to pay a word of tribute to the acting chairman. I think that perhaps save for his somewhat impassioned speech this afternoon all of us were quite impressed with his impartiality and his desire to see that all the matters referred to the committee were thoroughly explored. We all felt he was serving in a very difficult position. I personally felt that he did a very competent job, and I think I speak for all members of the committee when I say that we were impressed by the manner in which he conducted himself while he was the acting chairman.
However, Mr. Speaker, I really could not let his remarks this afternoon pass without dealing in some manner with his statements in which he referred to the action of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He said in his remarks that the member had turned loose certain allegations, and he talked about reputations being trampled into the ground.
Frankly I heard nothing which would indicate that, and I was hoping he would go on to tell us who was trampling reputations into the ground.
I do not think it is in any way reasonable to try to obscure the serious aspects of this committee report by attempting to assess any blame against the member for Winnipeg North Centre. I think it is significant that when he moved the motion to refer the hon. member for Labelle could hardly get to his feet quickly enough to second it, and the Prime Minister also was very anxious to second it. I think the house was convinced at that time that a prima facie case had been established, and the motion to send the matter to the committee was carried unanimously, without a dissenting vote. Therefore I think it is superficial to attempt to lay any sort of blame or otherwise upon the person who moved the motion.
However, Mr. Speaker, this was an interesting committee. It was both interesting and

dismaying, and it verged from the comical to the serious. The first lesson which it seems to me the house should learn is that generally speaking the committee on privileges and elections is not equipped in any way to deal with an issue of this kind. It was the first inquiry of which I had been a part where there were 29 prosecuting attorneys; where each member of the committee was free to go his own way, pursue his own investigation, ask any questions he wanted and endlessly repeat questions everybody else had asked.
I think it is significant that under the present set-up the committee is simply not equipped to do the job. There is no way for anybody to lead the questioning; therefore we spent days and days going over the same ground. The chairman's authority is far too limited in conducting such an inquiry and dealing with questions as they come forward, and there is a lack of any clearcut lines at all in an inquiry of this sort.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we had all the initial manoeuvring that took hours and hours and hours. It took a very long time to even decide what we were there trying to decide. Everybody had a different interpretation of the point of privilege, and it was a considerable length of time before we had any idea what we were trying to adjudicate upon. A great amount of time was spent in discussion trying to decide the order of witnesses and then, of course, we had the farcical, circus-like atmosphere that surrounded the lack of French reporters to take down the proceedings.
I do not want to review the terms of reference. The hon. member for Brant-Haldi-mand has already done that. We were trying to decide whether the statement of the hon. member for Labelle raised a question of privilege, and in doing that the testimony of the witnesses, of course, as has been pointed out, varied enormously. In fact the only thing the witnesses really agreed upon was that they met together on two occasions, once in a restaurant in Hull and once in the office of the hon. member for York-Scarborough. Other than that there was virtually no agreement in precise terms as to what had happened, what had been discussed, what had been agreed upon, what had been offered and what had not been offered. It was much easier to find out by the process of elimination those items that were not discussed than to find out what had actually taken place between the parties. So the evidence on the
Privileges and Elections Committee surface really does seem to be diametrically opposed.
But, Mr. Speaker, I think anybody who has dealt with this sort of thing before realizes one or two things. First, the most untrustworthy witness of all is the human memory. It is extremely difficult for anybody to recite in precise detail conversations and verbal statements that took place several months ago. This is why we terrible lawyers insist upon contracts being reduced to written form, and why international meetings insist upon written communiques. Once the meeting breaks up everybody's interpretation of what happened or what was said is probably quite different.
The other thing that I think it is important to understand in going through the hundreds of pages of evidence is that it is not just what is said at a meeting but also how it is said and the impression it gives. It is the interpretation that members take out of the words of other people who were present; and knowing Mr. Davey and how he can say things, I can see where some interpretation would be taken which might not be warranted.
However, Mr. Speaker, I think all one can do in these circumstances is to try to sift through the evidence, try to assess what really happened and then decide whether this does raise a problem of bribery or whether it does raise a question of privilege. I have tried to do this, and I hope in what I now say I will be fair to all parties concerned. After sifting the evidence and trying to reconcile the differences I think this is essentially what happened. I think the hon. member for La-belle decided that his political future was not very bright in the province of Quebec under the Social Credit party.

speechtext: Which group?

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The group to which he belonged at the time. That was his decision to make, rightly or wrongly. I think the hon. member then began to look for another home. He told us that his organizers in his riding instructed him it was their wish that he become a Conservative, and I think his own background led him in that direction as well. I think he then met these members quite by accident and communicated his decision to leave the Social Credit party and his desire and inclination to join the Progressive Conservative party.
Something he said or the way in which he said it led these members to believe that he was not of a firm mind. Consequently, with

Privileges and Elections Committee his consent or certainly without his objection, telephone calls were made and a meeting was arranged with Mr. Davey. Again, I think a similar procedure followed at the meeting. The hon. member for Labelle said he only went to the meeting to please his friends. His friends said that the fact he went to the meeting led them to believe that his mind was not made up.
Who is to say who is right in circumstances like that? Again, at the meeting at which Mr. Davey was present there was a great deal of discussion about a flag and about some other things, but memories are very vague as to who said what and what took place. Again I say that in the circumstances, reading the evidence and trying to correlate it, obviously something that the member for Labelle said or the way in which he said it indicated that he was prepared to listen. Things were said to him about joining the Liberal party or what he might expect or what his position would be, and either at that conversation or at some other time he was led to believe that certain things would be available to him in the event that he joined this party. He himself admitted that he expected future meetings at which he would be consulted with regard to whether he had pondered these proposals.
I know you cannot reconcile all the evidence, but looking at it as a whole it is pretty clear there was a discussion, and there were to be subsequent meetings. It is significant that after negotiations broke down the member for Labelle then approached the Progressive Conservative party and announced his intention to join. I do not believe the facts are really very much in dispute. I do not think anyone would quarrel with that and, speaking again for myself, I do not see anything particularly sinister in that sort of thing taking place.
But, Mr. Speaker, is there anything we can learn from this whole sad affair? I want to suggest six things that I think might be of some benefit to us in the future. The first one I have already mentioned, namely that the committee on privileges and elections is not equipped and should not be expected to try to judge between the accuracy of the memories of various members of parliament with respect to verbal statements and discussions that took place at meetings months before. It is difficult enough for an impartial judiciary to make decisions of that kind on verbal evidence, much less to turn over such a matter to a political committee that is

charged with all the partisan by-play that took place on the occasion in question.
Second, I am satisfied that there was no evidence of bribery disclosed. Certainly the member for Labelle never considered he had been bribed. Certainly the essence of bribery is the offer of something to corrupt. There was no evidence that anything had been offered to corrupt. Therefore I believe that bribery clearly is out.
The really sad aspect of the whole affair to me was the degree to which it showed how the two major political parties approached this matter. There was no discussion with the hon. member as to whether he believed in the principles of the Liberal party. There was no evidence that the program and principles of the Liberal party were even laid before the member so he could decide. All they talked about was nominating him and getting him re-elected; how the chances would be. Really, all they were after was another body on that side of the house.
To me it is a sad reflection on the way in which the Liberal party approached this whole matter. They were not interested in the philosophy or the principles of this gentleman in question. They never asked him whether he believed in the Liberal party. They just wanted somebody to go on that side of the house. I believe that is a sad commentary on the way in which this episode was conducted.
The chairman's ruling, of course, prevented us from going into the very interesting field of the negotiations which may have taken place on his entry into the Conservative party. Many members of the committee were anxious to explore this interesting aspect of the question. It was felt it was not germane; therefore we did not go into it.
The next thing is that I do not believe parliament should be asked to decide upon what are essentially political party matters. The occasion in question here was really something within the frame work of the political parties themselves. It never got beyond the vague organizing stage. I do not believe parliament should be getting to the point where we are mixing into the general political activities of parties. In many ways we try not to recognize parties as such in the house. All the members here have duties and responsibilities to their electors and to the country that vastly transcend any party partisan considerations.
I feel that one of the troubles here, therefore, was that this whole matter should have been dealt with on the party level. If Mr. AUGUST 17. 1964
Davey was to have been reprimanded, he should have been reprimanded by the Liberal party. This affair should never have reached the point where we as parliamentarians were wallowing around in a party mix-up that took place outside of the house.
Then I do not believe there is any point in referring this matter back to the committee for further discussion. I do not believe there is any way in which we could make a finding that would be of any greater help than the one we have made. There is no point, either in referring this, as I understand my friends in the Ralliement Creditiste intend to move, to the attorney general for consideration of perjury charges. There is clearly no evidence of perjury here. It would be taking outside the authority of parliament control over its own affairs, and this is something for which parliament has fought for generations. If any action should be taken, it should be taken by the house itself as has been done on other occasions.
As I have said, the only unpleasant aspect of the affair to me was the approach taken in which there was no real concern or discussion of the principles involved. Perhaps this is because there is not any real difference between the two major parties; I do not know. Certainly in my opinion this is the only real, sad aspect of the whole sad affair.

Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand for the manner in which he performed his duties as acting chairman of the committee on privileges and elections.
However, while several members of the committee were present, we objected to the adoption of the report, and that for a number of reasons.
First of all, some people seem prepared to sit on the fence. The hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Scott) has just said that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) was not sure he was going to join the Conservative party, while, on the contrary, the hon. member himself is reported as stating he was determined, even before the meeting, to do so. That is why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) seems to be blamed for rising on a question of privilege, when at that time everyone agreed.
But to discuss objectively the meetings of the committee on privileges and elections, we must keep to the statement made by the hon. member for Labelle and the question of priv-
Privileges and Elections Committee ilege raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Therefore, we must go back to April 27. Now, at page 2583 of Hansard for that date we read this:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
Last Friday, as reported on page 2538 of Hansard, the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Bechard) interrupted the debate to insinuate that my recent decision was due to political bargaining on my part.
The remark of the hon. member for Bonaventure could have passed for a joke, but the hon. member forgot that wit is the mother of humour.
I shall therefore take a few minutes in order to clear myself from the charge made against my integrity by the hon. member for Bonaventure. At the risk of disappointing members of the press gallery, I have decided not to mention the dates, places and names of certain Liberal members involved, because I refuse to become an accomplice of the chief Liberal organizer who would have allowed me to reflect on the political reputation of certain friends whose only mistake was to show their sincerity in this matter.
About two months ago, I met publicly four Liberal members in Hull. In reply to one of their questions concerning my political future, I said that I was quite decided to join the ranks of the Conservative party.

I appreciate that the Prime Minister denied it, but the hon. member for Labelle maintained his statement.
It is said that in the House of Commons, we must accept the word of an hon. member. Now, the hon. member for Labelle said one thing, and the Prime Minister said exactly the opposite. Where is the truth? It is rather difficult to know under those circumstances, and the truth should always be obvious.
As far as I am concerned, in view of the language used by the hon. member for Labelle, I cannot hesitate in believing the statement made by the Prime Minister. But since the matter was sent to the committee on privileges and elections, I think that the committee should have come to a clear conclusion instead of coming out with a most indefinite one.

Frankly, I admit that it left a bitter taste in my mouth to know that not only the Tories and Grits would contradict each other, but that the four Liberal members would do so too.

Therefore, a most vague and general conclusion is brought forward, which does not compromise anybody, in spite of the accusations that were made.

Davey, was one of his personal friends. We do not want to hear: It is because we had forgotten. It is obvious that if the hon. member for Labelle states that he was offered an electoral fund, he remembers that well because last time he did not have any and, moreover, he would need one for the next time.
The national organizer for the Liberal party and the hon. member for York-Scar-borough say: We never offered him an electoral fund. So, on the one hand, it is maintained that he was never offered one while on the other, he maintained that he was offered one.
On seven specific points the statements of two members are diametrically opposed, although they were under oath.
A newspaperman said: These can be called "apparent sworn contradictions" but in plain language this is called perjury. The members of the House of Commons are also here to set an example for the Canadian people. If a Canadian citizen perjures himself, he is condemned to prison; he is liable to prison under the Criminal Code. This section of the law dealing with perjury has been passed by the House of Commons. If there is some doubt as to a sworn statement made by a person, he will be prosecuted before the courts.
This is done in the case of high ranking persons, even in our judicial system. But anybody is considered innocent as long as he is not proven guilty by the courts.
When an ordinary citizen is involved, there is, at least, a charge laid against him, followed by an investigation and prosecution. But is there any difference when an hon. member is involved, who has to behave
Privileges and Elections Committee properly, or at least observe the law as passed by the House of Commons?
When a member of the House of Commons
is involved I think that it is perhaps neither more nor less serious, but it is nevertheless as serious as when an ordinary Canadian citizen is implicated.
There is an example to be set. Shall we begin to observe the law ourselves or shall we violate it without having to bear the consequences?
A while ago the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) said that the House of Commons -and not the attorney general of the province-would thus be authorized to render judgment upon its members. But will any member of the house, Liberal as well as Conservative, feel himself qualified to judge any action of his peers, when, from the first, he is imbued with partisan politics and will ask for nothing better than to deal in the worst possible way with a political opponent and do all he can for a friend?
To my mind hon. members in this house are not qualified to act in this way, but it is rather up to the judiciary to render judgment in such cases.
That is why we say that parliament should not ask the committee on privileges and elections to state that the hon. member concerned has committed perjury, but that everything be put in the hands of the competent authorities, that is, of the attorney general of Ontario so that the latter could proceed with an inquiry, go over the evidence and call in witnesses, after which he might render a decision himself without being politically involved like the members of the House of Commons would be.
It is true that parliament should as much as possible seek to direct its own affairs, as the hon. member for Danforth said, but in a case like this, parliament would be neither impartial nor objective, nor able to decide. Under the circumstances, the case should be left in the hands of competent and impartial authorities, that is, the judiciary.
Indeed, perjury in itself is not under parliamentary jurisdiction, but should be dealt with under the Criminal Code and the judicial system which, alone, have the necessary competence to render a decision with regard to perjury.
If there has been perjury, it did not happen in the house, but in committee. Then, the members involved accepted, of their own free will, to give up their privilege and testify under oath; they knew very well what to expect in so doing.

In my opinion, the situation at the present time is obvious. Throughout the country people have been informed of what transpired before the committee.
I have not the least intention to say who committed perjury. This is not my problem; it is not up to me to say. It is not up to us either. But it is incumbent upon us to point out the facts which took place. We do not want to decide by ourselves which one is guilty, and to what extent, but we believe that the House of Commons would fare better in the opinion of the public if the committee on privileges and elections were instructed by the house to leave the whole thing to the persons qualified to judge such cases. Then, people may have a better opinion of their representatives.
We are judging nobody, we are only asking that the facts be clarified to the satisfaction of each and everyone, and this not through prejudiced people, but through impartial people, whose task, entrusted to them by the parliament of Canada, is to see to it that the Criminal Code, and even the sections concerning perjury, passed by the parliament of Canada, be respected.
I am appealing to the members of the house, not with prejudice, since we shall have nothing to say then, but in an impartial way, so that parliamentary legislation, the reputation of the members and also the accuracy of the facts may be respected.

Mr. Speaker, the interview which Lord Thomson, formerly a Canadian, had with Mr. Khrushchev was, of course, a very interesting bit of news which came to us over the week end. We will want to give careful study to what Lord Thomson had to report about Chairman Khrushchev's proposal for important meetings after November next.

However, it is noteworthy that what the Soviet union, and Mr. Khrushchev in particular, had to say on this subject is conditional. It appears that the Soviet union has given an undertaking to Cyprus on a conditional basis. I think this underlines the vital importance of United Nations efforts to consolidate the cease fire, since in view of the position now taken publicly by the Soviet union it is more than ever obvious that a recourse to violence must at all cost be avoided. Second, the public position taken by the Soviet union points up the difficult nature of the political balance of forces in the security council.
I would not want to go beyond this without careful analysis of the statement and an opportunity of examining all the circumstances involved. But I thank my right hon. friend for directing the attention of the house to these important statements.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. Is he in a position to confirm or to deny the news to the effect that he forced Rear Admiral Brock, chief of the Canadian Navy in the Atlantic, to retire? Could he also give us explanations in that connection and tell us that the statements made by this officer during a sitting of a committee on national defence in Halifax are not the reason of his forced retirement?

Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National
Defence): Mr. Speaker, one consequence of the integration process is the fact that we now have on strength more officers than we have positions for. It is therefore necessary to retire some in advance of the normal compulsory retirement age. Rear Admiral Brock has a distinguished war record. He has served this country well and long. It is therefore a matter of regret that we have to retire officers of his calibre. I can assure my hon. friend that his retirement is in no way connected with the visit of the parliamentary committee or anything which may have transpired at that time.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: A supplementary question. I wonder whether I might ask the minister why this particular officer, who is one of the most outstanding of all of the senior officers in the Canadian forces, is being retired at the age of 51, with still four years of his normal service to go, with the consequent considerable increase in cost to the taxpayer through payment of his pension, when ordinarily he would have received his pay, which some other officer will be receiving in the meantime? It would seem a most peculiar way of dealing with senior officers in the Canadian forces-retiring an officer of this distinction at such an age, with the consequent loss of his abilities which are very necessary to the forces, and at the same time bringing about a great increase in the cost of the services to the taxpayer.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have indicated all along that it was necessary to effect economies in the Department of National Defence.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: There is no economy in that.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: As a result of the integration process we will be able to undertake our tasks quite satisfactorily with fewer people. This proposition has been widely applauded not only in this house but across the country. I do not think it was ever understood-I would be surprised if it was-that the reductions would only take place in the junior ranks; the reductions will take place right across the board at all rank levels. It is unfortunate that experienced people, whether they be of junior or senior rank, must be retired in advance of normal compulsory retirement age. The alternative is to keep on the strength of the Department of National Defence personnel for whom there is no further employment.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: Where is the economy in this action?

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: The economy is that there are fewer personnel required, so there are consequent savings which can be diverted to the acquisition of equipment. I think all hon. members agree that the cuts should be proportional throughout the rank structure, and not applied just to junior ranks.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: A further supplementary question. In view of the fact that officers of the rank of commodore and brigadier, and equivalent, have been and are being promoted to the rank of rear admiral, and equivalent, Which is the rank of Admiral Brock, how can there possibly be any savings by retiring a man four years before his normal retirement age, a man of outstanding abilities, and promoting somebody else from a lower rank essentially to take his place?

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two points I should make here. First of all, the total number of senior officers under the integrated service and as a result of integration at national defence headquarters will be substantially less. A lesser number are required and fewer will be on strength. In respect to promotion of some younger men, we have a problem which must be faced. Many of our best wartime commanders are coming to the compulsory retirement age at approximately the same time. There is some variation of course, but within a rather narrow band of years a very high proportion of the most skilled second world war commanders will reach compulsory retirement age. One thing we must do if we are to maintain the competence and the operational effectiveness of our forces through future years is to promote some younger men, some junior officers, to give them command experience so
Inquiries of the Ministry that they will be able to carry on the distinguished capability of the Canadian armed forces in the years which lie ahead.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF REAR ADMIRAL OF ATLANTIC FLEET
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the minister would now give us some definite reasons for this, I think, completely indefensible move, because all he has given us so far is generalities.

speechtext: May I direct a question to the Prime Minister. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the information I have received from those who are competent to advise on
6910	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry this constitutional and legal question is as follows:
It is true that the parliament of Canada, that is to say the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, did in 1952 enact a measure in direct amendment of the British North America Acts. However, the authority to make this amendment was conferred on the parliament of Canada by the British North America (No. 2) Act, 1949 which was enacted by the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the lords spiritual and temporal, and commons, assembled in the parliament of the United Kingdom.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF AMENDMENT METHOD AT DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext: What year was that?

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF AMENDMENT METHOD AT DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE
speechtext:
It was 1949. The authority of the parliament of Canada to amend the British North America Acts is therefore derived from and limited by this 1949 act of the United Kingdom parliament.
Any amendment outside the scope of section 91 (1) is therefore beyond the authority of the parliament of Canada, and must still be enacted by the parliament of the United Kingdom.
A further amendment to establish a complete amending formula, or to re-enact the British North America Acts as a statute of the parliament of Canada can, in my view, be made at the present time only by the United Kingdom parliament. Of course, if an appropriate amending formula were so enacted, a new constitution could be enacted pursuant thereto.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this most important debate and I make no apologies to anyone for occupying the time of the house with my contribution. I wish to say at the outset that I am going to speak in full support of the amendment and the subamendment.
I am fully aware of the gravity of the problem and of the gravity with which the people of Canada are beginning to look on this entire question. I am also well aware that my speech will not go down in the records as a great piece of oratory, nor will it be taken up by the press and radio and spread from coast to coast. It will not contain a great amount of research work on all the flags that have been flown in Canada. It may not contain the great principles that have been expounded by the leaders of the various parties, but I say in all honesty I regard myself as just an ordinary citizen of this country, and if in this debate I can convey to the house the feelings, thinking and beliefs of the ordinary man in the street, the man in the barbershop, the man in the bakeshop, the man in the corner grocery, the man who has been retired, the school teacher-all the men who form this great middle class of the people of Canada, of which I have the honour to be a part-if I can do this and convey their thoughts to the house, I shall feel I am justly fulfilling my responsibility as a representative of the Canadian people.

Canadian Flag
We have heard various speeches made in this house. We have heard a great deal from members who represent the great province of Quebec. I must pay tribute to these men because they spoke I feel, in all sincerity; they tried to the best of their ability to put forward the feelings of the citizens they represent concerning this flag question. They have been very eloquent and they have pointed out in no uncertain terms the feelings of the people of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, there are nine other provinces and today I propose to do the best I can to deal with the question as seen from my segment of Ontario.
Like many other members, I have prepared a flag speech. Like many other members I have spent weeks in research on this subject, knowing its importance to Canada and to the Canadian people. I do not intend to use that speech today. I say this because I have been in my riding and in other ridings in northwestern Ontario in the past few week ends talking with the people on the streets and trying to find out what they think of the actions of parliament and of the government in connection with this matter. What do I hear on every street? The ordinary Canadian says: What in the world is going on in Ottawa? What concessions are we making to the province of Quebec? Are we, in fact, making concessions? We hear talk of a federal state of Canada. We hear talk of a republic. We hear talk of changing the names of various crown corporations. What is going on? We in Ontario have the right to know. What do the people of Quebec want? Where will it end? These are the questions the people in Ontario are asking today. This is what they are saying. They are asking: Have these people from Quebec a grievance? Is it a grievance which has grown up over the years? Can we meet and solve this problem? How serious is it? The very citation is predicated on the assumption that when you have an amendment to a question debate is restricted to the amendment as being a substantive question. It is only in the case where an amendment is in the nature of an alternative that, as the citation says, the debate that follows is not restricted to the amendment. 202 (1). To an amendment, when proposed from the Chair, an amendment may be moved; but only two amendments can be proposed at the same time to a question.
(2) As the proposal of an amendment to an amendment originates a fresh subject for consideration, the new question thus created must, to prevent confusion, be disposed of by itself. An amendment, when undergoing alteration, is therefore treated throughout as if it were a substantive motion upon which an amendment has been moved. The original motion, accordingly, is laid aside-
The original motion accordingly is laid aside. -and the amendment becomes for the time a separate question to be dealt with, until its terms are settled.

-I shall show that there has been a mad shambles made of the business of this parliament; that there has been hypocrisy in the claim which is made for the desire for legislation; that this government did deliberately misrepresent the facts to the people regarding a distinctive flag; and that the utter chaos and impasse this parliament is faced with today can only be laid at the doorstep of one man, and one man only-
Diefenbaker.

-who in a statement to the radio stated-no, I am speaking of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of this govern-

ment now in power. This man said on the radio in an interview that it would be unfortunate if this question was made an election issue because it would cause an unfortunate division in the country. How naive can a leader of the country be when he believes that this will not be an issue in an election, whether that election is held three months or three years from now. I have never experienced a time when the Canadian population, especially in my area, has been so aroused over an issue as they have other this one.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, are they in favour of the red ensign? They show in the most determined way that they are in favour. They believe that the only way this matter can be solved is by a plebiscite. For in spite of the legal arguments put up by government speakers that there should not be a plebiscite, I am of the opinion that since this issue was deliberately placed into partisan politics by a political party, the only way that we can get it out of politics and have a responsible decision made is by letting the people of the nation decide the matter for themselves.
Are they in favour of the red ensign? We have had claims of all kinds made in this house. Who is to know whether 83 per cent favour the red ensign or 3 per cent favour the red ensign? Who is to know whether 83 per cent favour a distinctive flag or 3 per cent favour a distinctive flag? We have heard claims made in this house, but have we any valid proof of them? I have heard hon. members opposite say that the ethnic groups in this country are solidly behind a new flag. I challenge this statement, because I have spoken, both in my own riding and in other ridings, with members of ethnic groups and I find that this matter is a sore subject with them. Many of these people come from countries where it is said that the disintegration of symbols and the taking away of traditions has been the first step in the downfall of a nation, the first step in a loss of independence. They do not want to see this happen here. They see this as a danger, and when hon. members opposite stand up and tell me that the ethnic groups are in favour of a distinctive flag-this distinctive flag-I challenge them to furnish me with some proof. So far I have not heard or seen any.
Then we hear the claim that the youth of the nation are in favour of a distinctive flag. This is a deliberate misrepresentation. I say to you, sir, that the youth of this country are in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag

when the question is put to them; but the question "Are you in favour of this distinctive Canadian flag?" is never put to them.
I have had only one letter from a student, who told me that gentlemen are coming round to his school and asking: "Are you in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag? If you are, Canada should have one; write to your member of parliament and say that you want to support Mr. Pearson's flag". Mr. Speaker, is this the support that the youth of the country are giving this flag? I say that this is deliberate misrepresentation. The very fact that these people say "a distinctive flag" and not "this distinctive flag" causes me to think that there should be a plebiscite. Let the people decide between the flags. Let the people make up their own minds what they want.
I can appreciate the position the government is in. I can appreciate why the government does not want a plebiscite; it is beginning to realize the awful truth-that perhaps the majority of the people in the country do not want this Pearson flag. What a horrible position this issue has placed the government in. And if I ever had respect for the parliament of Canada it is now, Mr. Speaker, because with a power group in this House of Commons determined to impose this flag on us, and with the realization that perhaps the majority of the people of Canada do not want it, here in parliament a determined opposition has a chance to make itself heard -that is, if we are not placed in the position where we cannot debate, where we are limited in debate, or if we are not held down in the manner we experienced this afternoon.
Order.
We want to get the facts on the record, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is now making a reflection on a ruling by the Chair confirmed by the house.
I suggest he confine himself to the question before the house.
Mr. Speaker, I will, of course, abide by your ruling in this matter. But the fact still remains that when we want to put facts on Hansard we run into trouble. And why? Are the facts damaging?
Order.

Is this government afraid of the truth? Can they not stand on their own feet? Can they not take the credit for doing great things for Canada? Are they afraid?
Canadian Flag
Do they think the flag issue is of such magnitude that the government is going to stand or fall on it? Is this what they are afraid of? Is this why we are having violent opposition to this flag?
I will deal with another point: Are you in favour of the three maple leaves flag?
Hear, hear.

Hon. members opposite applaud. If the people of this country want or could want the three maple leaf flag, why must the government put on a public relations campaign to sell this flag? We speak of the traditions of the Canadian flag. What tradition can be found on the posterior of a bikini bathing suit on television? What tradition can be found on a blanket of a racehorse? What tradition can be found on the dresses of three college students? Are these the traditions of the Canadian flag we are asked to adopt? Is this the way?
This afternoon we heard in the house about
100,000	bumper stickers. Is this the way we earn a Canadian flag? This is college calisthenics. This is in the same category as the colouring books, the pigeons and all the rest of it. The people of Canada will not accept this.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Simmer down.

Order.

Mr. Speaker, I will change my words. I will say that I wish to thank the minister because if it had not been for her remarks about the Canadian red ensign, remarks which ensured my re-election to the House of Commons, my campaign would have been much more difficult.

Oh, oh.

I am
sure the hon. member would not want to continue too long in this vein and will soon get back to the resolution before us.

On a phony point of privilege.
