speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the question of privilege, I remember no occasion, except for one which was a private matter, when my hon. friend was present at any meeting at which I was present. I assume my hon. friend knows the rules of the house and that when he makes such remarks he makes them on his honour, and challenges remarks which I make on my honour as a member of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly prepared to let the matter drop. The minister has made her statement and I have had the opportunity to make my statement. I rely on my statement and if necessary will furnish proof of my statement. Mr. Speaker, because of the fact statements have been made that this is a deliberate concession to the province of Quebec, because statements have been made that the government has sold out, because all these statements cast doubt on this country of ours and could create a division, I sincerely believe that the only way in which these doubts can be resolved is to have a plebiscite based on the subamendment and let the people show whether or not they are

in favour of this new Canadian flag. I am convinced that the people of the province of Quebec are unjustly accused-
Hear, hear.

-because all they are doing is asking the government to live up to its campaign promises, and nobody in Canada should be penalized for that. Unless we have a vote of this nature we have no idea whether the majority of people in Quebec, Ontario or any other province are in favour of this flag or the red ensign, or a combination of compromise, or perhaps the one maple leaf flag.
I am very sincere and most serious about this matter because, as I have stated before, the people of Canada are very much concerned about the outcome and about the way the matter has been handled. Too many people are being unjustly accused of acts for which they are not responsible. There are accusations and counter accusations and this problem must be solved. Here in parliament we must find a method of solving it that will work to the advantage and meet the wishes of the majority of the Canadian people.
If the people of Canada are given a chance to make their views known I believe they will not accept one flag of one man, of one particular party. There is too much of the future of Canada at stake. I am absolutely amazed at the number of people in this country who are concerned about the fact that any man in Canada would dare to remove the crosses from the Canadian flag. Why do they want to remove the crosses? People take a very serious view of this. Where are we going in the design of this flag?
May I say I hope a way can be found out of this impasse. Let the people decide. Is the government afraid? Do you not dare to let the people decide?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think that the decision which was rendered, appealed and confirmed after appeal, is so fresh in our minds that we have no reason to have forgotten it and we should not depart from it. Under that decision the question is not whether or not we should have a plebiscite.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is a matter which is theoretically assumed on the basis of the decision. The only question is, granted we should have a plebiscite, are the four questions submitted in the subamendment proper for inclusion in the questionnaire? I submit

respectfully that all discussion of whether we should have a plebiscite instead of a vote by the responsible members of parliament is out of order on the basis of the decision rendered this afternoon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the point of order we heard the ruling this afternoon and Mr. Speaker read from Beauchesne. We do not need to repeat those passages. I have read Beauchesne as well, and the rule says that when there is a motion in front of the house and an amendment and a subamendment the main motion in effect is set to one side, the amendment becomes the substantive motion and the subamendment is in amendment of that. According to the rules the amendment plus the subamendment are the subject for debate-
No.
That is what you argued this afternoon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -so the hon. member is within his rights in talking about the value of a plebiscite.

This is the second time I have been interrupted. I have tried to abide by the ruling and keep directly within the terms of the subamendment. I would say this. The subamendment asks if you are in favour of the Canadian red ensign or of the three maple leaf design. We have heard hon. members state why they are not in favour of the red ensign. I listened to their deliberations quite respectfully in silence, because I was interested in hearing their views. I have come to the conclusion that when they make their choice they will be doing something that no enemy of Canada has ever been able to do, that is lower the red ensign.
Shame.

I will go one step further, Mr. Speaker. I can say when they make their choice I will be wondering if it is not pure irony that the mad pursuit of this change will settle nothing. The province of Quebec will still fly the flag of Quebec; the province of Ontario will still fly the red ensign; the province of Newfoundland will fly the union jack and British Columbia will fly the union jack. This is an impasse. This is a horrible situation in which Canada finds itself. I hope there will be statesmen in this house who will stand up and say what they believe is best for Canada rather than what is best for a local headline.
Canadian Flag

At
this stage of the debate, Mr. Speaker, I should like to put forward a few of my views on this question, a question which should be at least of some concern to all Canadians. I am very much aware that it is of vital concern to a great number, and the indications that I have received from my part of the country are to the effect there is little or nothing wrong with our present flag. As a matter of fact, it has been and still is flown very proudly.
It is a matter of regret that this question has come before the country at this time when some elements seem to be in a state of unrest with regard to racial and economic matters. It seems to me that changing our flag at this time, especially in the manner that it is being pursued, will not ease tensions or create unity. Much of our national and historic pride is wrapped up in historic symbols which are now displayed on our flag, the Canadian red ensign.
I cannot believe that the majority of the people of this country wish to destroy the symbols and historic attachment for those symbols for which so many young men and women suffered and gave their all. I do not suggest that these young people went to war only because of a flag. They did so to fulfil their heartfelt obligations to the principles they have inherited and went quite prepared to lay down their lives to defend them. If the youth of this country feel that these historic symbols are no longer important, and I do not believe for one minute that they do -as a matter of fact, indications reaching me are to the contrary-then it must be because our educational system has failed to indoctrinate them with an appreciation of what has gone before. After all, education is an accumulation of what has been revealed in the past.
I was born in this country and under our present flag. During my lifetime, I have experienced some of the difficulties which one would expect to encounter in a growing and changing country. However, never once have I blamed these difficulties on my forebears, or the symbols which they produced. I still have to be convinced that the offspring of any race, whether born in this country or adopting this country and truly understanding the principles for which our symbols stand, would willingly seek to destroy them.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, some compromise is necessary and, as a legislator, I must not close my mind to this possibility. But in the light of the strong feelings evident on the measure which is before this house today, I

Canadian Flag
beg of the Prime Minister and his government that they reconsider this matter. After all, I am sure that if those with strong views had an opportunity to air their views and to hear the strong views of others, no matter how contrary, all concerned would feel much better.
Before this house at the moment is an amendment and subamendment. These two amendments taken together, if accepted, would refer the choice of a flag to the people themselves. Since the people already have a flag, there is no urgency and a plebiscite could be conducted conveniently and without cost, during the next federal election.
In closing, I again appeal to reason, because in this case time is not necessarily of the essence. Should this house vote on this matter without the expression I have referred to and our symbols of the past disappear, I shall deeply mourn their passing. I commend to all people words which are contained in the new brochure of parliament issued on the occasion of Canada's recent birthday. I quote:
Walk proudly through the home of all our freedoms. Feel yourself welcomed. Stand silently amid the brave, proud ghosts of men who forged our nation. Look thoughtfully on word-drenched walls, thick with a hundred years of history. Breathe deeply of an air that is, to you and yours, the very breath of life itself-for being Canadian, your breath of life is freedom. Guard carefully this heritage, that freedom's house may stand.
I emphasize the last line by repeating it:
Guard carefully this heritage, that freedom's house may stand.

Mr. Speaker, I had decided some time ago to take part in this debate and I thought it would be useful to prepare some remarks on the general scope of this subject concerning a national flag and the events that led to the present situation.
However, since there was an attempt to stifle us and since the situation has changed a little, I shall, therefore, change my speech.
Now, I accept the ruling given by the Chair although I do not agree with it at all. The Chair can impose a ruling upon us but not its reasoning. Therefore, I hope the house will not have cause to regret the decision made this afternoon. Let us get back to the subject now before us.

Just in case somebody has some observations in regard to what they feel are the limitations of this afternoon's decision I would suggest that the first paragraph of the

subamendment be read and it will be seen that the subamendment cannot stand by itself. It says:
-that in such a plebiscite among the questions to be placed before the people should be the following-
There is a reference to a prior clause. There is full discussion of a plebiscite "and that such a plebiscite" should contain certain questions.
Notwithstanding the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) there is no doubt whatever in my mind that both the amendment and the subamendment may be discussed, and that was the purport of the ruling, that the discussion should be relevant, and that is what I intend to be and what my colleagues intend to be.
During the course of certain remarks this afternoon it was indicated by some hon. members that they felt there had been sufficient discussion. Hon. members opposite are quite prompt to try to close down debate. We see comments in the press and elsewhere; and across the way they use that word "filibuster," which sounds so nice. But you know, Mr. Speaker, there are those in a democratic regime who believe in freedom of speech. Hon. members opposite profess they believe in freedom of speech as long as they are speaking or they intend to speak, but if anybody else wishes to express an opposite point of view, then of course the discussion is closed. These comments were made this afternoon and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is right to comment upon them. I have said what I want to say about them, but let it be quite clear that I reject them entirely.
I would like to hear the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh) and a lot of others get us and speak on this question, and that brings me to the question, why a plebiscite? Do hon. members feel that they themselves are expressing the views of their constituents, that because of certain personal characteristics-

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think it is my duty, so long as it seems quite clear that the ruling made by the Speaker is not being respected and applied, to rise on a point of order, and I shall so long as I think I should. The decision which was rendered by the Chair this afternoon, and which I repeat was appealed and confirmed on appeal, was to the effect that the discussion is to be limited to the subamendment. The only question before us presently is whether or not, if there should be a plebiscite, it would be in order and appropriate that

the four questions submitted by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) be included in the questionnaire. This is the only point before this house, and what the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has just said is that he intends to depart from the ruling which was rendered this afternoon. I submit respectfully on the face of his very assertion that any part of any speech in the house which does not concern that particular question ought to be ruled out of order.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I reject entirely the argument of the Minister of Justice, and if he would read the subamendment he would see the word "plebiscite" is contained in it, and that is what I intend to discuss.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It was the feeling of the Chair that the remarks being made by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) at this point were rather of an introductory nature and that he would get to speak to certain aspects of the plebiscite in due course. That is why the Chair did not feel it should intervene at this point. I know the hon. member who has the floor, now knowing the purport of the decision rendered by the house this afternoon, will want to abide by it.

I think I fully understand the purport of the ruling this afternoon as well as the Minister of Justice. I also think I know my rules a little better than he does.
In so far as the plebiscite is concerned, I maintain that the Minister of Justice himself is not one who can personally say that he can determine for the people of his constituency that there shall be one design, and that one design only shall be the flag of this country. I fail to see how an hon. member, on such a matter so personal to himself and to the people, can say that the flag shall be one design and one design only. That is all that is being presented to us. This, in essence, is the only choice before the members of the house, either to accept the flag or bring about the downfall of the government.
The Minister of Justice may think he has curbed debate as a result of what he did this afternoon, but what he has done is actually to split speeches into two or three, because these points will be brought out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: At the proper time.

Well, if the minister was trying to improve, or sort of get the debate
Canadian Flag
moving along, I can assure him from experience that what he has done is merely going to reverse that.
Is that a threat?

The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) asks, is that a threat. He used to sit over on this side and we could hear him quack quacking from the top of the fence. That is what he is doing now. He is not even in his seat. Let us not hear from the Minister of Fisheries.
In so far as what should appear in a plebiscite, the first question we propose is, are the people of Canada in favour of the red ensign? That is a very simple question. It is not like some of the polls that were taken during the course of the last few months which asked, "Are you in favour of a red ensign as against a distinctive national flag?" They did not say what was a distinctive national flag. It was the red ensign against the field. That is one question we are asking, and from the mail I have received I can assure hon. members that there are great numbers who insist upon the red ensign. They have the right to do so, the same way as other people have the right to insist on another design.
I do not wish to force a design on any person. This is something which is personal, something which derives from family antecedents, the part of the country in which one was brought up, or in which one now lives, or perhaps because of military experience. I myself was profoundly impressed by the red ensign this summer while with the maple leaf tour in June from Caen to Nijmegen. I attended the ceremonies at the Vimy memorial and on that particular day, and in that particular setting, with the Canadian red ensign flying across the Vimy memorial, the effect was most moving. It was a proud flag, joined there with what is possibly the proudest memorial to the men of this country who gave their lives for freedom. It was a symbol of Canada. That is how it struck me on that occasion.
Hear, hear.

The red ensign was flying, also, at the cemeteries in Normandy, in the Pas de Calais area, at Ypres-all historic names-as well as at the cemetery where my own comrades lie. Then again, it was flying at Canada square in Dieppe and at the Dieppe cemetery.
This is how it affects some people. I will admit there are others who do not share these sentiments. My mail indicates a di-

Canadian Flag
vergence of opinion. It is predominantly in favour of the red ensign, though, as has been shown by other polls. But I come to the conclusion, and I have tried to be as fair as I can, that the division within the country is very close as between the red ensign and a

I repeat the word "a"-distinctive national flag. Thus, if the three maple leaf design which is now proposed by the government were to have support of only 55 per cent of the people of the country, or 51 per cent, does this mean it is likely to command the support and affection and the loyalty of the rest of the people of Canada? This is what bothers me with regard to the division which has been indicated during this debate.
I have been talking about the red ensign. The next suggestion is a modified form of red ensign showing the British connection by the union jack and the French partnership in this country by the symbol of the fleur de lis. This may be one form to be considered. There are others which are proposed. We have seen a great number of designs combining the union jack with the fleur-de-lis on a red background. Let it be known that the red background gives a certain dignity and, shall we say, posture to a flag which is not apparent in many other designs.
The third design mentioned is that put forward by the government, the three maple leaf design. This whole flag business has been introduced at this time in order to give the country what some people have sought, namely a distinctive national flag. But we have to look at the word "distinctive". What does it mean? I looked it up in Webster's dictionary. The definition given is "Distinguishing from others; characteristic". Take the first meaning-"distinguishing from others". Is it suggested that the red ensign is not distinguishable from others? I have here a chart of the flags of 110 nations, members of the United Nations in December, 1962. If we look at this chart from the point of view of whether the red ensign is distinguishable from others, let me say there is not one flag that approaches it. This cannot be said for many other of the flags which appear on this chart. I could show hon. members many instances where there are almost identical flags with colours reversed or a slight change in design. Here they are-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. May I bring to the attention of the hon. member that it is not customary in this house to use documents, or exhibits, if I may use that term, of the type the hon. member is now using. He showed this exhibit and the Chair said noth-

ing. But I know he would not wish to use it extensively. The hon. member might refer to a recent ruling of Mr. Speaker when flags were exhibited in the house. At that time Mr. Speaker ruled that they should not be so exhibited. I feel it would be very bad practice if members were to bring into the house for the purpose of supporting their arguments exhibits of the type the hon. member is now using in his speech.

I realize certain difficulties which might arise if flags were spread all over desks, as was done on the occasion of the recent ruling, but I think a comparison between bananas and oranges is being made here. On the other hand, I am faced with a printing problem. I could ask that this chart be appended as an appendix to Hansard but the colours would not come out and therefore I could not make my point.
I have a list of the similarities here but I shall not go into the details. May I simply indicate that many of these flags are similar in appearance. And I am talking now about national flags; I am not talking about merchant marine flags or secondary flags where there might well be similarities. After all, because of the limitations imposed by the designs themselves, there are bound to be some similarities.
Let us consider the other part of the definition-"characteristic". Take the three maple leaf design. First of all, I am told on good authority that this is a botanical impossibility. Let us consider whether this design is characteristic of all Canada. I am only repeating an argument which is well known, but-
Mr. Speaker-

Oh well, I know the hon. gentleman is the authority who put them together. May I suggest that the maple leaf is not characteristic of Canada as a whole. It is only characteristic to a limited region of the country. I think one could make as good an argument that because the buffalo once roamed in millions and millions on the western prairies, yet did not exist in eastern Canada, the buffalo is as characteristic to Canada as a whole as the maple leaf is to Canada as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, there is some difficulty in arguing that the maple leaf is characteristic to Canada as a whole.
Why did the Meighen government recommend that the maple leaf emblem be adopted?
You have already had the opportunity of making a speech.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the hon. member why the Meighen government recommended to His Majesty, King George V, that the maple flag-three leaves on one stem-should be the emblem of Canada?

I feel there is some difficulty in associating some of these representations with any particular party or government. If one looks back to the antecedents of the red ensign one will find them in the time of Sir John A. Macdonald, and in various forms until 1904 when it was taken down by a minister in the Laurier administration. The hon. member has referred to a particular administration and I will mention another. The red ensign was taken down and replaced by the union jack during the Laurier administration.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to discuss the aesthetics of the maple leaf design. I should like now to deal with the fourth alternative. Perhaps I should not refer to it as an alternative because my hon. friend, shall we say a linguistic purist, suggests that the four choices should not be considered as alternatives, and I concede him that point. In any event, I find the fourth choice, the single maple leaf design, preferable to the three leaf design. Unfortunately the three leaf design has been supported by what I consider to be a very artificial argument, that is, that one leaf represents the Anglo-Saxon population.
Nonsense.
One leaf of the three leaf design represents the Anglo-Saxon side, one leaf represents the French side and the third leaf represents the other people of Canada.
Nonsense.
It was your own Postmaster General who used that argument.
He was wrong.

You say the minister was wrong, and I agree with you. This argument is a most artificial and unsupportable one, yet is the one that has been trotted out on occasion by the government to buttress this choice.
Oh, no.

Mr. Speaker, the reasons I have given, make it possible for me to believe a far better and more acceptable design is that of the single maple leaf which represents unity of Canada. I would think far bet-
Canadian Flag
ter of something which represents oneness or unity in Canada than of something which will permanently imprint a division in the minds of the people of Canada.
It would only do so in your mind.

Mr. Speaker, someone suggests it would only imprint this division in my mind, but I suggest that was the reaction to the argument used by a government spokesman in respect of the choice of this symbol.
I think the official opposition has been eminently fair in putting forward these four choices. We have not rejected the choice of the government. We feel it should be put forward to the people as one of the four choices. The opposition has accepted as a choice a design with one maple leaf, which seems to have had its most enthusiastic sponsorship from hon. members to my immediate left. We have also accepted the red ensign as a choice. We have accepted also a modified form of the red ensign. We have done so in order to give the people of this country a chance to have some features included which they would like, and eliminate others which they feel should not be included. I think the opposition has been eminently fair in regard to the four choices.
I find myself, representing a large and populous riding, in a great dilemma in so far as the choice of a flag is concerned. Mr. Speaker, I conducted a poll in which I asked the constituents of my riding the following questions: Are you in favour of the proposed maple leaf flag? Are you in favour of the red ensign? Are you in favour of some other distinctive national flag? Those questions reasonably approximate the questions to be put to the people on this plebiscite. I chose the individuals to whom I wrote in this regard in an attempt to have a good cross section of the constituents from the standpoint of age, income level, ethnic origin, religion, urban and rural, yet answers were quite clear. In so far as the question in respect of a distinctive flag other than the red ensign, of approximately 100 people answering, 48 were against and 38 were in favour. In so far as the question regarding the red ensign, 58 were in favour and 32 were against. Approximately 60 people were against the adoption of a maple leaf design and 25 were in favour.
I also asked whether this whole question in respect of a distinctive Canadian flag would be divisive or promote national unity. Of ap-

proximately 100, 75 thought it would be divisive and 25 thought it would promote national unity. The people contacted were evenly split as to whether a referendum should be held or not.
Mr. Speaker, I think the poll I conducted was very fair. A national poll has indicated that more people are in favour of the red ensign than of an unknown distinctive national flag.
Mr. Speaker, I feel the many other points I wish to speak on should be reserved for another occasion. I should like to say this, Mr. Speaker. We have given a fair choice to the people of Canada. There was no choice offered. I should say there was a choice: Take it or leave it.
On that note, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe the people of Canada should be asked to adopt a flag on a take it or leave it basis, and it is for that reason I ask hon. members to support the subamendment.

Someone has said that no question since that old contentious question years ago out west- the execution of Louis Riel, who incidentally would not have been executed had he not previously caused Thomas Scott to be hanged-has been more controversial in this divided country than the question of this Canadian flag. I am sure you would agree that that is true. I am not taking a pessimistic view of the matter, because I think in the end good thinking and the proper use of compromise in the interests of all the people concerned will prevail, and that we will work out a solution to this contentious question.
Today this modern question of the flag is born of the same reasons that that old question out west was born. The former controversy, now far back in antiquity, was a needless development. It was born of bad politics, of hatred, of one man's lust for power and a certain amount of misunderstanding. A lot of those things apply today in this debate. Some men become so imbued with a lust for power that they are determined to ride roughshod over the sentiments, civil rights, institutions and emblems of God fearing citizens. Is it any wonder that this party, the Queen's loyal opposition, is taking an active part in this debate when these dangers are present? Riding roughshod-that is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is trying to do, and will do, if he can get away with it. His politics- those of the Prime Minister and his party- are bad at the present time, Mr. Speaker. He

and his party as well as all other parties promised the people a distinctive Canadian flag.
At this point I want to cite the bad politics, the shiftiness, the deception finally and actually implied in this promise. The people of Canada-and X mean the majority of the people of Canada-calmly agreeing in the last election campaign to this, did not expect the resulting so-called distinctive flag to be one from which both the union jack and the fleur-de-lis would be absent. I am sure that every hon. member here will agree that that was not the general expectation of the people of this country. They expected to see those two old and honoured emblems, the union jack and the fleur-de-lis, on the promised so-called distinctive flag. But what a political play hon. members opposite have made of that word "distinctive", Mr. Speaker. Did Your Honour-

I swing back to clause 1, "are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign". What a play they have made on the word "distinctive". According to the dictionary "distinctive" means "marking a difference or separation". That is an ominous explanation, for by playing on the word "distinctive", which has been endlessly repeated by the Liberal party for the past year or so, they have certainly marked out a separation in this country. That honoured flag, the Canadian red ensign, is more than distinctive. It might better be termed "distinguished". It marks out no difference or separation in this country but nobly represents the symbols, aspirations and personal patriotism of every citizen of Canada.
What are the attributes of this distinguished flag? What are the synonyms of "distinguished"? Prominent, conspicuous, noted, glorious, illustrious and famous. Hon. mem-

bers will agree that right here on the hill the appreciative lenses of thousands of cameras are pointed every day to capture the glory of this flag high up on the peace tower.
I swing to clause 3 of the subamendment, "Are you in favour of the three maple leaves design"?
Yes.

This reminds me of a comparison that took place right out on the east lawn. On the day that the Prime Minister authorized the trial flying of his flag, the three maple leaves design, on a special pole in front of the Senate, a friend of mine, Mr. Brian Blackstock of Toronto, a schoolteacher, was showing two university professors from Texas the sights of parliament hill. They inquired as to what the meaning was of this flag flying on a pole while at the same time the Canadian red ensign was flying on the peace tower. Their comment was: Surely you are not going to adopt this for your country's flag in preference to the beautiful banner flying from above. They said that to them the new flag looked like the flag of one of the emerging nations of Africa or resembled a flag of commerce, advertising a product for sale.
Soap flakes.
Imperial oil.
Molson's ale.
Canada Packers.

The youth of Canada, many of whom know the meaning of the component features of the red ensign, are asking the government and parliament especially to maintain this distinguished flag as the flag of our country. There are thousands of our people, especially those who in their youth have been boy scouts, girl guides or wolf cubs, who have learned the meaning of this flag and its features. They have learned to honour and respect this flag. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, who the base, arch conspirator would be on the right hand side of this chamber over which you preside who in years past has told the youth of this country and indicated to them by the example of action and use, "This is your country's flag flying over this hill and the public buildings across the country, the Canadian ensign", but who now says "This is not your country's flag; I have another one which I ask you to honour from now on". This is just like taking good parents away from a child, substituting another set of parents, and asking the child immediately to

love and honour the new parents while the real ones still exist.

Hon. members opposite may laugh, but I think it is a good comparison. The youth of this country say, do not give us a meaningless flag; do not give us this pale creation which is one man's choice.
This is the reason we need a plebiscite.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

I was talking about the request of the youth of this country to give them a live flag, a flag that could grow with the country. They say, do not give us a dead flag. This trifoliate flag cannot be added to. The three maple leaves on the white background are confined by the two blue bands at the end. This flag cannot grow. Whatever heraldic balance it possesses, that is the way it must stay down through the ages. We need a flag like the red ensign that has evolved, grown and developed with the country and whose make-up can accommodate further growth. The Northwest Territories and the Yukon will soon be provinces, so some day these provinces will need symbols on our flag.

Paragraph 3, Mr. Speaker, asks, are you in favour of the three maple leaf design? In looking over this scheme of collusion between the government and certain provincial components of the country, I note that hon. members on the government side have been most anxious to get the Prime Minister's flag through as quietly as possible. They reveal themselves by their own, individual actions. Orders have been given to their back benches: Do not debate the question; let the opposition founder against our rocks of silence; when the opposition carries on the debate long enough, then we will accuse them of obstruction. For some time now Liberal strategy has urged members to keep quiet regarding the flag, and this has been illustrated tonight.
Paragraph 2 of the subamendment asks, are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign and changes made thereon to show the main heritage of the founding races? We are urged not to say anything to hurt the feelings of Quebec because of the fear of dividing the country. Now, Mr. Speaker, how deceptively naive can you get? How deceptively naive are the occupants of the government benches? How gullible do they think we are? How gullible do they think the rest of the country is? There is a cause for every effect and this debate, no matter how long it may take, is the effect of a cause. The cause is the bad performance, the deceptive politics of this government. The cause has already divided the country as it has never been divided hitherto and the scars will take many years to heal.
Referring to paragraph 3 again, Mr. Speaker, and the three maple leaf design, I may say this:
Canada is often portrayed as a muscular Jack Canuck in high boots, tight breeches, khaki shirt open at the chest, and felt hat, a doughty, durable, indestructible character, the twentieth century epitome of the pioneer, and the indomitable spirit that built this country under the surveillance of law and the union jack and red ensign. But this portrayal is not the true Canada. Canada is fragile, as the Prime Minister has lately learned. Canada is a 4,000 mile assembly of many races, many regional interests, many creeds, each often on a different curriculum, but of course all studying at the same school of life, Canada, and of many varied economies, but all working together. That is what we should be doing here.
The Liberal party has hurt Jack Canuck and the picture of Jack as I have just given

it. It has hurt this country and now, by this ill founded flag measure the Liberal government proposes to inflict more wounds on Canada, wounds that may never heal. I say to the Prime Minister, "Stay your knife, let the noble banner that with faith, justice, patience and charity helped build this country continue to wave over us and we will go on to greater unity and greater accomplishments." Yes, Mr. Speaker, I believe that in the end we can work out something that will suit all the people of this country.

I should like to point out to the government if they would avoid capsizing on the shoals of fact, that Canada is only as strong, as united, as unanimous and as happy as are the several provinces. One of the provinces namely Manitoba, in disagreement with the position taken by the government regarding the flag has already named the red ensign as its provincial flag. Seven other provinces are flying the red ensign from all their public buildings and their citizens fly it from the verandahs and rooftops as never before. Newfoundland, as is its ancient and honourable usage and custom flies that great and respected banner, the union jack. What is the reason? They have finally come to life. They have realized they are in danger of losing this emblem which is so dear to

them and which has meant so much to their fathers and mothers down through the years.
I respectfully suggest to the government that the value of the opinions of the premiers of the provinces be recognized in deciding this vital national question. The government need have no fear of politics being a factor in present circumstances when four of the provincial governments are Liberal, four are Conservative and two are Social Credit-a very fair balance sheet which I think would yield a lot of wisdom. I suggest this should be done even if it should be decided to take a referendum. Let us first have the advice of these men. They could help select a flag which would take nothing away from the recognition of either of the founding peoples.
I have here an article from the Ottawa Journal of Wednesday June 17, 1964. It states:
The Prime Minister appeals for everyone to accept the decision of parliament, whatever it is. But there will be more chance of general acceptance if the flag of Canada is selected with reflection and careful choice. Democracy demands that dissenting voices be heard before the will of the majority prevails-
This house tonight does not seem to be too willing to grant this democratic privilege.
-perhaps including the method suggested in these columns on June 3-a postponement of decision long enough to allow a meeting of premiers and party leaders to give their views on the flag. Our thought was that even should such a conference fail to attain unanimity it would enable the federal government to demonstrate clearly it had sought unanimity.
I am in favour of the amendment and of the subamendment, particularly of the paragraph which asks: "Are you in favour of the Canadian red ensign?"

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have to interrupt the hon. member. I may say his time expired some five minutes ago but he was given this additional time in view of interruptions and points of order which were made while he was speaking. Unless he has the unanimous consent of the house to continue his remarks-
We have suffered enough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret the hon. member cannot continue without unanimous consent and there definitely is not that.

Sometimes I wonder, with all due respect, whether the House of Commons is here to decide the affairs of this nation or whether we are simply here on a hair-splitting expedition. This man Beauchesne is a very learned gentleman, but I do not think his book was ever written in order to throttle debates in this house. I do
Canadian Flag
not see how we can discuss the subamendment and the amendment unless we talk about the substance of what we are here to talk about, that is, the flag.
The people of Canada want to know-and this is what they ask me in almost every letter I get-what we are doing about the flag. This is a subject which usually is too hot to handle. Politicians shy away from the subject as a rule. They are not shying away from it tonight. You can see they are not. We intend to attack this problem until we know what we are fighting about. So, with permission of the house I want to tell hon. members what this flag means to me. I cannot argue in a vacuum. I cannot tell others what it means to them. But I have a right to say what it means to me and I know I speak for at least a million Canadians when I do so. I do not wish to parade my war service but after all I cannot deny my origins. I cannot deny that I am of British origin. When I am speaking about a flag would you ask me to say that I am willing to give away a tradition of my race? The British people are a proud race.
That is right we are.

One of the reasons we are a proud race is that we face every difficulty that comes before us in a chamber such as this with free discussion, with kindness and with patience, and we make positive contributions. It is very difficult to make a positive contribution when emotions are aroused and we lose our tempers and call each other names. This institution was not based on that kind of performance and it has stood for
2,000	years.
One of the things this flag has stood for, Mr. Speaker, is this institution. We are allowed to take part in a free discussion in this chamber, and I say to you that if you allow this freedom of discussion to be stopped by closure, by booing and catcalling, or by calling each other names, this institution may well become a great Stonehenge-a circle of silent stones, and freedom will be wept for at that grave.
I have visited Stonehenge on the island of England. Perhaps Stonehenge is a circle of silent stones now because freedom died in Britain 3,000 years ago and was reborn under the Christian cross. I do not know whether people believe anything any more, or whether any of us believe anything.
The origin of the cross in this flag lies in the fact that Joseph of Arimathea took our Lord and Master down off the cross. He knew what a cross was. He saw the Son of

Canadian Flag
God hanged on a cross. He took that body down and is the man who supposedly brought the first cross to Britain 2,000 years ago. I am not a hairsplitter or a quibbler but let us say he brought the first cross to Britain
2,000	years ago.
I am not a history teacher but a Canadian, born on a homestead out west. In case you think I am a displaced person perhaps I should state that I have a little native blood in my veins. I have this native blood in my veins because John McKay, who came out to Canada with Alexander Mackenzie, married a native out in western Canada. That was seven or eight generations ago so there is no need for you to be superior. Do not bother to look up your own family trees.
My grandfather was a Hudson's Bay factor at Lac la Biche in 1874. I will not go back in my family's history further than that.
We are just envious.

My grandfather loved these native people and treated them fairly. When the natives burned down the fort they spared him and his family because of his honest and square dealings. This took place in the days of Louis Riel. Louis Riel believed in the British crown. Why should those who scream about Louis Riel being such a patriot now desire to do away with the British flag and the British crown? Why should they want to create another Stonehenge? Do not forget that the British crown and flag stand for the first cross brought to Britain 2,000 years ago.
I will not vote for any flag that denies to Canada the heritage of the Christian cross. The fact that there are three crosses in the union jack and in the corner of the red ensign does not make those flags any less loved. The red ensign was the flag representing a union of the cross of St. Andrew and the cross of St. George in 1801. We also included our Irish friends because we have always admired them. Most of Britain's good soldiers were Irishmen, including Montgomery and Alexander. Many Irishmen saw fit to fight many wars under the British flag.
I am not a waver of the British flag as the last word for democracy or freedom, but I say this, that under the British flag more freedom has been spread across this planet than under any other sign. I challenge you, one and all. Which of you who want to pull down our flag and trample it in the dirt v/ould dare to go across the line and suggest they should take their "glory" down and trample it in the dirt, and expect to live. Are we going to be something less than the land

of the north and the land of the free? We are all very quick to jump to our feet, throw out our little chests and show our visitors from the south our fishing holes and our important resources. What is our most important resource? I suggest our most important resource is our love for freedom and for fair play. That is our greatest resource.
Do any of you remember what happened to Uncle Tom, or do you remember Uncle Tom? Uncle Tom knew where to find freedom. He found freedom under the British flag. You want a distinctive flag for Canada.
I suggest we have a distinctive flag. I say we now have the most distinguished flag on this planet. I do not put our flag ahead of my country. Our flag is only a rallying point. Our flag was at that place where the Van Doos and the First Field Regiment stood side by side on the battlefield.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order.
I should like to continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, please.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Closure.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon.
member who has the floor will realize that when another hon. member rises on a point of order he should be heard on that point. The Minister of Justice has risen on a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As everyone will agree, we would really have closure if I were not allowed to express my point of order.
Make sure you have something to say this time.
Shut up and listen.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not wish to repeat the argument that was made this afternoon, but I should like to suggest very respectfully that the debate now is directed toward a question of what would constitute a proper questionnaire to be put to the people of Canada if there is to be a plebiscite. We are bound in this regard by the decision rendered this afternoon by Mr. Speaker. That decision was appealed and confirmed on appeal. We are presently limited by the Speaker's decision in which he made the distinction as between that decision and the previous one rendered in respect of the principal amendment, stating that we are not concerned here with an alter-

native and, therefore, not concerned with the merits of an argument as to whether the red ensign is a distinctive Canadian flag. We are concerned with questions to be properly included in a questionnaire to be put to the people. So long as we do not discuss the matter of the drafting of the questionnaire but instead attempt to discuss the merits of the principal question we are out of order, as ruled by Mr. Speaker as recently as this afternoon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to the point of order. The Minister of Justice has stated we are concerned with questions to be included in a proposed plebiscite. Surely in discussing those questions to be placed on a plebiscite an hon. member may give reasons why those questions should be included, and that is exactly what the hon. member has been doing.

Mr. Speaker, there is nothing I like better than to be challenged in my own field. I happened to take the trouble to obtain some legal training, before coming to this house, in anticipation of running into this type of argument. In every statute on our books one will find an interpretation clause. I am sorry I must use the facilities provided by an interpretation clause before referring to the meat of my subject. I have yet to get to the meat of my subject.
If I have not done so already, I should like to explain, what a flag means to some people, because some people I know do not know what a flag means. Mr. Speaker, I am using an interpretation clause to speak on the point of order. I am attempting to give a lawyer's answer to a lawyer. If you would like a citizen's answer to a citizen I invite you to stand up and tell me what a flag means to you and why you think the Christian cross should be removed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Has the hon. member concluded his remarks on the point of order?
Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe the point raised by the Minister of Justice is well taken. On the other hand, I think the argument made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) has substance also. But we are definitely bound by a decision of the house made this afternoon to the effect that we should discuss this specific matter relating to the plebiscite.

Mr. Speaker, I am trying to be fair and lucid, and I think most hon. members are able to follow my argument. But
Canadian Flag
what is a flag without history? How can we say whether or not we will have a plebiscite if we do not know what a flag is? A flag is a rallying point for all national sentiments. The national sentiments of those of British origin are very strong, but they are not exclusive. Let me take my lawyer's training again and say that Canada is not one nation. Canada is a legal entity consisting of two main races of people joined together with an evolutionary system of government. The events which occurred on the plains of Abraham in 1759 no longer count. It does not matter who won the battle.
It does.

In the treaty of Paris in 1763 Canada was ceded to Britain, which perhaps is an unfortunate truth. That may have been an unfortunate event in history, but I claim that by 1864 we had reached another stage in the evolution of our country. In 1864 the Fathers of Confederation met at Charlottetown, and I gather there will be another meeting there shortly to commemorate that event. I hope that the hundred years since 1864 have not been without their value. I hope that when this meeting takes place we will take another look at this legal entity of ours which we call Canada and which we hope will be a nation, and perhaps at that time we will reaffirm what one might call our marriage vows.
I for one have always been willing to meet Canadians of French origin on an equal footing. In case I am called to order I am talking about our dual heritage behind our flag. I am taking great pains to try and learn la belle langue frangaise and I shall continue to do so until I can converse as fluently in the French language as I can in my own.
I would submit that we are not in fact two different races of people, in the sense of being black or white, or distantly related. I think it can be said that the French and English are very closely related indeed, if not by actual blood certainly by culture. Their respective cultures have intermingled so much that it is hard to tell where British culture ends and the French starts. I am sure that many of us on reading our school history books were moved to tears at the story of Joan of Arc. I would be proud to have the flag of Joan of Arc incorporated in any Canadian flag.
Who wants it?

I would want it. That is why I have the right to stand up in this house. My family happen to be of Norman-English blood. My name in Norman-English is spelt "Bygge"

Canadian Flag
and means "barley". After a thousand years we are proud of our dual ancestry in Britain. Here in Canada after 100 years we are proud of our dual ancestry in Canada.
I am not trying to stir up strife here, Mr. Speaker. I am asking for co-operation. I am asking for the same level of brotherhood which is always being talked about and for the right to give my side of the story. One of the reasons I am proud of my British heritage is because I am also proud of our French. I do not think we can build a nation in Canada unless we take this attitude and are willing to forget the plains of Abraham and the last hundred years of bickering. Why not start now on August 17, 1964, and cut that out and get down to brass tacks? But we are not going to get down to brass tacks, any more than we did on the plains of Abraham where we used cannon, unless we sit down and talk things over. The battle of the plains of Abraham was 200 years ago. Have we learned nothing in 200 years? We failed with cannon, so let us get together and compromise.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I am talking of the dual cultures.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may be talking of dual cultures, but I think the dual culture part of his speech should be related to the plebiscite and to what questions are to be put on the plebiscite.

Mr. Speaker, if hon. members do not know what a flag is, how can we decide that matter? I believe that the people of Canada do know their flag, because I have travelled through Ontario this last week and seen thousands of flags flying. Yesterday I went to Belleville and in a store there I saw being sold over the counter the Pearson pennant. There was a great big sign two feet square outside saying: "The flag of Canada".
Shame.
Now, it may well become the flag of Canada. I for one will be the first to serve that flag if and when it is ratified.
Hear, hear.

I said if and when. But I say to hon. members opposite, do they think they have the right to make the decision, if they have not the courage to stand up and say why? I am not afraid to stand up and say why. There are 15,000 people in my district of French ancestry or of French relationship and a great many of them are proud of the present flag, the red ensign. I am willing to

take a democratic vote in Canada on any design. I believe in democracy and my ancestors have believed in it for 2,000 years, ever since the dignity of man was once and forever held up before God and man-the Christian ethic. I should like to hear someone stand up and tell me-I would much prefer it was the Prime Minister-why I must take down the present standard as my standard of behaviour.
Read Hansard.

They took Joan of Arc's flag down. They put her lily banner in the dirt, and she was only a woman. But what a glorious woman she was. She put her lily banner out in front and never looked back, and with her very small army swept the ranks clear. She put the rightful heir, I am led to believe, on the throne of France. Then the king of France ratted on her, and you know the rest. Now she is a saint. Which of those opposite in their male pride will stand up and say that they think the lily banner of France or the cross of St. George should be laid in the dirt?
I am not running down, Mr. Speaker, homemade designs. I know where the flag was made. I know who drew it. He has boasted about it openly. He is the man who gave us a new flag. It was given to a man with great courage and determination, a man brave enough to put an economic gun to our heads and say: "Take this flag or you will lose your $18,000 a year". But my dear fellows, do you think there is any amount of money that would make me sell my flag or my country? They hang their heads and say: "Isn't that drivel?" But it is not drivel to me or to the
30,000	men who may never see the flag again. Are they going to rub it off all our national monuments?
We will rub you off.
Oh, oh.
Stand up and say that. Stand up and say it.
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege-
Have I the floor or haven't I?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has the floor but the hon. member for Cape Breton South is rising on a question of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member on the other side who made that threatening remark should have the courage to stand up, identify himself and repeat it, or is he ashamed to do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not utter the remark, but one thing that is running out is the opposition's sense of humour.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Athabasca.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think anything we can do can destroy the parliamentary system, no matter how we mistreat it. It has lasted too long. But I do appeal to hon. members to put their petty opinions to one side. If you have not got the courage to stand up and ask for a free vote and if your leader has not got the courage to allow a free vote, then we have no alternative but to put the matter to the people of Canada in a plebiscite. This is the substance of the matter. We are down to it now. Have we not got the courage to stand up on our own feet and say what we think? We have just had a glorious example of the lack of it. I would not like to think that kind of behaviour was typical of any segment of our population. I know that the people in the galleries and the people throughout the country are not ashamed to stand up and say where they stand on the flag and I want to give them that opportunity.
Some might say, when did you dream this up? I have never sidestepped the question of the flag. In Hansard for January 21, 1962 you will find a 20 minute speech by me on the subject. I begged hon. members then and I got little response. So I am not being partisan in this matter. I think we have all been delinquent. We all know what our flag has been and we might as well have ratified it 100 years ago. French Canada has always been proud of her allegiance to the British crown, at least in the last 100 years, and if they are not now, then I say stand up and say so. This is a free country. That is one of the advantages of being a Canadian.
Do those people who talk about secession really want to secede? I am sure Newfoundland does not want to secede. All the people there want to do is to retain their British traditions. Joey Smallwood told you that in no uncertain terms and you had to change your original resolution. Many people across the country admired the Prime Minister temporarily when he said: I will come out and cut the Gordian knot; I will give you the opportunity to make a nice clean decision on the flag; I will offer you this flag so that you can clear up the issue once and for all, so that you can stand up and be counted and be Canadian.
That sounded fine, but when Joey did not like it a two-headed resolution was brought
Canadian Flag
forward. Now we are going to have two flags. If you go to Britain and talk to the Queen you wave the union jack but if you are somewhere else you wave something else. Is this the way to be united? I am sure there is not one member in this chamber who does not believe in democracy and if we had a free vote and the vote was 51 to 49 I am sure we would all stand up and sing "O Canada", salute the flag and say God save the Queen. If this is not so I am very much misled. I am in the wrong company if this is not true. This is what I thought when I first came here and this is what Joey Smallwood thought when he led his loyal little island into confederation. He said: We will now become part of the brightest star in the British crown. He meant that. Don't think Joey didn't mean it. He is not going to be nice to you boys if you do away with the flag. You know that, so you have backed down.
Now you are ready to back down, for what? Is it for the $18,000 and the splinter groups because you have not got the courage to stand on your own feet? Oh, they are going to bring in an amendment and you are going to vote for it because that is the only way to save your political future.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.
If the Conservatives have nothing but stupid things to tell the house over and over again, it would be better for them to remain seated, because we are ready for the question.
Their filibustering tactics are detrimental to the interests of the Canadian people. I am getting sick and tired of the Conservatives.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There is no question of privilege. The hon. member for Athabasca.

We have the first question in the suggested plebiscite, will we retain the red ensign? Of course we should. Second, should we have a modification? I do not like backing down at all, but I certainly put my country ahead of my own personal opinion and pride. I would say that if we must have a modification of the flag I love in order to keep Canada one I will vote for it. Third, should we have the three maple leaves flag? I see little merit in it though I like the maple leaf. We used to sing "The Maple Leaf Forever" and it was a term of derision. A lot of people in Canada did not like it. But what did we of British origin do? We abandoned any

Canadian Flag
idea of making it our national anthem because it divided us and we have adopted "O Canada", a French Canadian song with very-strong religious overtones. We have compromised and accepted that, many of us perhaps with heavy hearts, but those who want to see a greater Canada and who love this country will take "O Canada" and sing it with that much more enthusiasm 'because it is one of the beloved songs of our French brothers. We have compromised. I do not think there has been one word said in any part of the house against that decision.
I for one would like to see a package deal and have national service also. Some will say: Oh, this is an old soldier speaking and he cannot forget. No, it is hard to forget the friends, the volunteers I served with. It is very hard to forget and I will not forget them. But I am not going to put sloppy sentiment ahead of the unification of my country. So I say that if the majority of members of the house in a free vote will stand up and conscientiously say that they honestly want to do away with everything we have had in the past, that only with this new flag can we march on as a fully united country, that every man jack, be he native North American or French or English, will rally to these colours and if needed will give up his time, his money and loved ones, put them all on the table and say, "I will go", then I will accept that decision. Some enlisted because they were unemployed but I will not say that about my friends. I will not say that about the ones who did not come back. I will not say it about the boys in bomber command. I will say this to defend myself, which I rarely like to do. If I am the only yellow one in the family it is a peculiar thing because in my father's family there were four brothers, one of whom was in the British navy, one in the Strathcona Horse, one in the South African police and my father was in the mounted police. I have three brothers. My oldest brother was in the Royal Canadian Air Force. Let us keep them flying. My second brother was in the Royal Canadian Navy, the senior service, and my youngest brother was in the R.A.F. I myself tried to fly and could not qualify so I had to go into the lowly artillery.
I appeal to the soldiers and non-soldiers. I really believe we do need symbols. We do need a rallying point. There are times when nothing else but the sight of the old flag rallies you out of the dirt, and not the flag on a pole like the hon. member for Edmonton West said. No, you do not go in for flying

the flag, but you fly it somewhere. You fly it deep down inside you where it cannot be got at when you are darned good and scared. There are no heroes in battle. You land on your face in the mud but you still get up and go on again simply because you marched into school 15 or 20 years before singing "O Canada" and looking at a little piece of red bunting flying at the masthead.
Do not ask me to turn my back on it, to forget it and never look at it again. If we have to have this new flag I want you to do this much at least. Parade a man from every regiment in Canada that ever served under the red ensign and let them march to the peace tower and lay the red ensign away with glory where it belongs. Do not let it down and say that it means nothing, because it means a great deal to a lot of people.
I do not like to have to talk like this. I do not want to have to go to the widows of this country and say that we have no flag. The people in Holland know that we do. All you have to do is take out one of these little flags about three inches square and show it to the people in Holland. They will crowd around you like a bunch of chickens for a crust of bread; they will be glad to have you back. You should have seen the tears running down their faces when we went into Amsterdam. Where these little flags came from I do not know. The people waved them in Amsterdam. You say, what battles were you in? Everybody cannot fight battles, but we can all be patriots. Is there something smelly about that word now? When nurse Edith Cavell died, she was not ashamed to say "Patriotism is not enough". Do you know what she meant?
Order.

What would you like to order? If you people really want me to sit down, I will. The single maple leaf design is only a political compromise and everyone in this chamber knows it. There would be nothing wrong with accepting the triple maple leaf if this would unite us. If it is going to unite us, if you are going to serve it, then there is nothing wrong with accepting it.
You laugh at the Legion and say they have no right to this flag. Are we taking it away from them? Were they all drunks? Were they all unemployed? Are they all drunks now? They were drunk with patriotism once. I am not willing to compromise on the single maple leaf design. I am not willing to take the triple maple leaf design on the

basis of my own choice. However, I say again, and I will keep on saying it, that I am willing to bow to a democratic choice. If each and every one of you can stand up on a free vote and vote for this then I challenge you to request your own leader to do so.
I suppose that the four questions listed are good enough for a plebiscite. I honestly believe that if the people of Canada have this choice, then the first question will win on the first ballot. If there is any way of satisfying our Canadians of French origin I am certainly willing to do that. I have nothing but love and admiration for these people. They are our flesh and blood. The fact that they have a rather difficult and beautiful language should make no difference. We follow branches of the same religion, at least. Here again, I think we have had an evolution in religious thinking. If they had had an ecumenical conference 500 years ago, who knows, there might never have been a division in the Christian church.
We have listened to one of our members here speak about nihilism and materialism; taking everything out of the flag and having nothing left. I think there may be something in this modern psychology which is attempting to do away with our standards. If we lose faith in each other we stand to gain nothing. I am one who has always stood for individual enterprise.
Order.

Is this not in order? It is the essence of our British culture just as I am certain it is of our French culture. The French are making a great contribution to our country. They are alive in the arts. They are intensely proud of their origin. I say if there is any way of giving them any more recognition, if there is any way we can cooperate to the slightest degree to make them forget the errors of the past or even the facts of the past, things we cannot undo, then I am in favour of that because we can certainly march on into the future together.
Let us have this referendum. If these four questions are not satisfactory, then perhaps we could consider others. I have thought about them and I cannot think of anything else which would improve them. We who are here have done a great deal to cloud the issue. We have said things, perhaps, that we should not have said. We have made this issue partisan, whether we want to or not. This applies to both sides. The only fair way is to go to the people and let them make this 20220-439
Business of the House
decision. I do not think it is necessary to have an election. There is a great deal of work we should do. I do not make this statement out of fear I assure you. You can look up the record. I think it would be a waste of time. I am sorry that no longer is the crown allowed to be the independent referee it used to be in the old days. Now the power to call an election rests in the hands of the Prime Minister. We all know this has been the case since 1925. It is up to him. There is no purpose served by looking at the Leader of the Opposition and saying, you fellows can force an election. The Prime Minister holds this stick and everybody in Canada knows it. This stick is being used, and I think it is an unfair one. I do not believe the flag should be a partisan question.
I have been giving you my own views. I have not been directed by any other member in this chamber. Perhaps some of them would have liked it better if I had not said some of the things I have said. However, there are times when if you do not speak, the very rocks cry out. I take full responsibility for everything I have said. I meant every word of it. I assure you that if we can find some flag design which will unite our country, I will be the first to vote for it and I will be the first to serve that flag when it is decided upon.

Mr. Speaker, it should be obviously a time of excitement when a nation is choosing a new flag. The fact that this is not possible should be abundantly clear to the whole house. The reason I make this statement is something I want to follow up, but I see the clock and it is 10.30.
